# Savings {.unnumbered}

<br>

**Savings** are the bridge between earning and investing; they're the third of the four levers introduced in the [Foundation](foundations.qmd). In this part of the book I'll cover how much to save, where to keep it, and how to make the whole process [automatic]{style="color:#48a56a; font-weight: bold;"} so willpower isn't part of the equation.

## Savings and the Financial Order of Operations {#sec-savings-foop}

Once you know your income and have categorized your expenses, the next question is: **where should your available money actually go?** To answer it, we'll lean on Brian Preston's **Financial Order of Operations (FOO)**.[^foo-budget] The FOO is a fixed sequence of nine steps, each one funded before moving to the next.[^savings-foop]

[^foo-budget]: We introduced the @sec-foo-intro in the [Budgeting](budgeting.qmd) chapter and again in the @sec-foo-debt section of [Managing Debt](managing_debt.qmd).

[^savings-foop]: See the full guide at [moneyguy.com/guide/foo](https://moneyguy.com/guide/foo/) [@preston2024foo].

| Step | Priority | Why it comes first |
|----|----------------------|--------------------------------------|
| 1 | Deductibles covered | Cash on hand for your insurance deductibles avoids new debt from a routine claim. |
| 2 | Employer match | Free money from a 401(k)/403(b) match beats any other use of the next dollar. |
| 3 | High-interest debt | Toxic-rate debt compounds faster than any investment; see [Managing Debt](managing_debt.qmd). |
| 4 | Emergency reserves | 3–6 months of essential expenses in cash; see [Emergency Fund](emergency_fund.qmd). |
| 5 | Roth IRA / HSA | Tax-free growth, funded while your income still qualifies. |
| 6 | Max-out retirement | Push tax-advantaged retirement accounts to their annual limits. |
| 7 | Hyperaccumulation | Taxable brokerage investing once retirement accounts are maxed. |
| 8 | Prepaid future expenses | Kids' education, a down payment, or other planned large costs. |
| 9 | Low-interest debt | Extra payments on mortgages, once everything above is funded. |

The FOO isn't a budget; it's a strategic framework that tells you [what to do with the money your budget frees up]{style="color:#48a56a; font-weight: bold;"}, one step at a time:

* **Steps 1–2** establish protection and capture free employer money. This reflects Bogle's low-cost principle: free money (the employer match) beats any other use of the next dollar. 

* **Steps 3–4** eliminate dangerous debt and build emergency reserves. Morgan Housel's insight applies directly here: before your savings can grow, they have to be protected from emergencies.

* **Steps 5–7** fund tax-advantaged and taxable investing for long-term growth. Ben Felix and Bogle both emphasize what makes this stage work: sticking with the plan (behavioral compliance) and keeping it simple.

* **Steps 8–9** handle planned future expenses and low-interest debt payoff.

In this part of the book we'll focus on steps 1–4, which all involve *saving* before investing. Steps 5–7 (the investing side) are covered in the [Investing](investing.qmd) part. Throughout, we'll follow Sethi's principle to [pay yourself first]{style="color:#48a56a; font-weight: bold;"}: automate your savings before you spend anything, and willpower drops out of the equation.

## Principles for Consistent Saving

The chapters that follow lean on five voices in personal finance that I trust. Here's what I've taken from each of them about building a savings practice that actually works:

**Morgan Housel** (behavioral finance): [*Consistency beats optimization.*]{style="color:#48a56a; font-weight: bold;"} A modest savings rate you keep up for 30 years outpaces aggressive saving you abandon after 18 months. Before your savings can grow, they have to be protected from emergencies.

**Ramit Sethi** (conscious spending plan): [*Pay yourself first.*]{style="color:#48a56a; font-weight: bold;"} Automate your savings before you ever see the money. Once saving no longer depends on willpower, your only job is to spend intentionally on what's left.

**Ben Felix** (evidence-based investing): [*Behavioral compliance matters more than perfect strategy.*]{style="color:#48a56a; font-weight: bold;"} A budget or savings plan you follow imperfectly beats one you abandon. The best savings rate is the one you can keep up.

**John Bogle** (simplicity principle): [*You don't need complex tactics.*]{style="color:#48a56a; font-weight: bold;"} Low-friction systems that work beat sophisticated ones that don't. Free money (the employer match) beats any other use of the next dollar.

**Brian Preston** (Financial Order of Operations): [*Prioritize ruthlessly.*]{style="color:#48a56a; font-weight: bold;"} Every dollar should flow in a fixed sequence: protection, then employer match, then debt elimination, then emergency reserves, then investing. Know the order before you start.

Here's the practical sequence we'll follow:

  1. Build a starter buffer (covered in [Emergency Fund](emergency_fund.qmd)).
  2. Pick a target **savings rate** ([Savings Strategies](savings_strategies.qmd)).
  3. Park the money where it actually grows ([High-Yield Savings Accounts](high_yield_accounts.qmd)).
  4. Automate the whole flow ([Automating Savings](automating_savings.qmd)).

From there, the money is ready to feed into [Investing](investing.qmd).
